title: IB History Extended Response: A High-Mark Method
summary: IB History extended response strategies for decoding prompts, planning in two minutes, building analytical paragraphs, and checking essays under pressure.
body_markdown:
A strong **IB History extended response** does not begin with everything you know. It begins with a decision: what does this question require you to prove?


Under time pressure, that distinction matters. Students often remember plenty of history but write around the prompt, producing accurate narratives without a sustained argument. Higher-mark responses do something different. They interpret the command term, establish criteria for judgement, select relevant evidence, and explain how that evidence supports a conclusion.


The practical method is simple:


- Decode the command term and scope.
- Turn the question into a precise argument.
- Build a two-minute paragraph plan.
- Use evidence to analyse rather than narrate.
- Address complexity or alternative interpretations.
- Check the response against the relevant mark scheme.


The details vary by paper and syllabus. The current course remains in assessment through 2027, while the revised IB History course receives its first assessment in May 2028. Confirm which specification applies to you. The underlying essay discipline, however, remains remarkably stable.


### Decode the question before recalling content


Imagine opening the paper and seeing a familiar topic. Recognition creates relief, but it can also create a trap. The mind starts retrieving rehearsed material before it has understood the task.


Slow down for a few seconds. Break the question into four parts:


- **Command term:** evaluate, discuss, examine, compare, or another instruction
- **Topic:** the historical development being investigated
- **Scope:** the specified states, leaders, region, period, or examples
- **Debatable claim:** the proposition your response must test


Suppose a question asks you to evaluate whether economic conditions were the most important cause of a political development. You are not being asked to list economic causes. You must judge their importance, compare them with other causes, and explain the standard used to decide what “most important” means.


That standard might be immediacy, long-term influence, breadth of impact, or indispensability. Defining it gives your essay a spine. Without criteria, evaluation often becomes a collection of unsupported adjectives such as “major” or “significant.”


The[RevisionDojo guide to IB History exam preparation](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/comprehensive-guide-to-preparing-for-the-ib-history-exam) can help you distinguish the demands of different papers before applying this method.


### Build an IB History long answer plan in two minutes


A two-minute plan is not a miniature essay. It is a set of decisions that prevents expensive confusion later.


Write a provisional thesis first. It should answer the question directly and acknowledge the strongest complication. For example:


> Economic instability created the conditions for change, but political weakness was more decisive because it converted public dissatisfaction into an immediate collapse of authority.


Next, sketch three analytical paragraphs:


1. The factor named in the question
2. The strongest competing factor
3. The relationship between factors, or a counterargument that tests your thesis


Beside each paragraph, note one or two precise examples and the analytical point they prove. Do not attempt to empty your memory onto the page. Evidence earns its place by doing a job.


Finally, write two words beside your plan: **judgement** and **link** . They remind you that every paragraph needs a reasoned conclusion and a connection to the exact wording of the question.


For repeated planning drills, use the[IB History essay planning guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/mastering-ib-history-essay-structure-and-planning) alongside the[IB History Paper 2 Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-history/ib-history-paper-2-750-1500/questionbank) . Planning becomes faster when you practise it separately from full writing.


A student questions a historical fact about how it supports an argument


### Structure paragraphs around claims, not chronology


The safest paragraph structure for an IB History long answer is not a rigid acronym. It is a chain of reasoning:


### Make a comparative claim


Begin with a sentence that answers part of the question. “Economic hardship contributed to unrest” is relevant but limited. “Economic hardship widened unrest, although it became politically decisive only when the government failed to respond” establishes a relationship and prepares evaluation.


### Select precise evidence


Use accurate evidence such as policies, events, decisions, dates, developments, or relevant historical interpretations. Precision matters, but volume does not automatically create quality. Two carefully explained examples are usually more useful than six facts left without analysis.


### Explain the mechanism


Ask the question many responses skip: **How did this evidence produce the claimed effect?**


A policy may have damaged legitimacy. A military defeat may have exposed institutional weakness. A leader’s decision may have accelerated an existing crisis. This causal explanation turns knowledge into analysis.


### Test the claim


Consider a limitation, alternative factor, or contrasting case. Then decide whether it changes your judgement. This is not the same as adding “however” before an unrelated fact. Effective qualification sharpens the argument.


### Link back to the question


End with a comparative judgement. Explain why the factor was more important, less important, more immediate, or more fundamental than its alternatives.


The[RevisionDojo essay structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-history-essay-structure-7-worthy-response) explores how to adapt this framework without forcing every question into the same template.


### Use evidence as proof rather than decoration


Historical facts can feel productive because they fill the page. Yet evidence without explanation is like a witness whose testimony is never connected to the case.


After each example, ask:


- What does this prove?
- Why did it matter?
- How does it affect my judgement?
- Is there evidence pointing in another direction?


This produces a useful rhythm: claim, evidence, explanation, evaluation. The response keeps moving intellectually rather than merely moving forward in time.


Different perspectives can strengthen this process, but only when they are integrated into the reasoning. Naming a historian is not automatically analysis. Explain what the interpretation emphasizes, how it differs from another explanation, and whether the available evidence makes it convincing.


RevisionDojo’s Study Notes can help consolidate context, while Flashcards strengthen retrieval of dates, examples, and terminology. AI Chat can then challenge you to explain why a fact matters. The goal is not to outsource the judgement. It is to practise making the judgement yourself.


### Write an introduction that commits to an argument


A useful introduction can be short. It should define any disputed term, establish the scope, and state a qualified thesis.


Avoid opening with a broad history of the period. The examiner already knows the background. Your task is to show that you understand the debate created by the question.


A strong thesis should be specific enough to guide the essay but flexible enough to survive your own evaluation. If your paragraphs reveal a better judgement, refine it in the conclusion. Historical argument is not weakened by nuance. It is weakened by contradiction that goes unnoticed.


### Check against the mark scheme, not your feelings


A finished essay can feel fluent and still remain descriptive. Use the final minutes to perform a targeted check:


- Did I answer the command term?
- Did every paragraph address the stated scope?
- Is my thesis visible throughout the response?
- Did I explain how the evidence supports each claim?
- Did I compare factors or interpretations where required?
- Does the conclusion deliver a supported judgement?


For the specification assessed through 2027, the top Paper 2 generic markband, worth 13-15 marks, emphasizes clear focus, effective organization, accurate contextual knowledge, critical analysis, integrated evaluation of perspectives, substantiated points, and a consistent conclusion. The revised course first assessed in 2028 changes the assessment structure, so students should use the correct specimen materials and criteria. RevisionDojo’s guide to[IB History essays under the 2028 specification](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/why-ib-history-essays-are-different-under-the-new-specification-first-assessment-2028) explains that transition.


The important lesson is broader than any one markband. Do not ask only, “Did I include enough facts?” Ask, “Did I use relevant facts to sustain the judgement this question demanded?”


### Practise the complete process under time pressure


Essay technique becomes reliable through a cycle of attempt, feedback, and correction. Choose a prompt from the Questionbank, plan it in two minutes, and write it in Exam mode without opening your notes. Afterwards, use RevisionDojo’s Grading tools to locate unsupported claims, weak links, or descriptive sections.


Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can extend this into full timed practice. Study Notes and Flashcards repair knowledge gaps, while AI Chat helps interrogate your reasoning. The Coursework Library can provide broader models of historical argument, and RevisionDojo Tutors can offer human guidance when the same weakness continues across several attempts. The[guide to earning a 7 in IB History](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-history) offers a wider revision framework for connecting these resources.


The best extended responses rarely come from knowing every fact. They come from controlling the facts you know. Decode the task, choose an argument, build analytical paragraphs, and finish with a judgement that has earned its confidence.


Start with one prompt in RevisionDojo’s Questionbank. Then sit a timed paper in Exam mode. What feels slow today can become a calm sequence of decisions by exam day.
